title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

reading.body:
This is a case of a literary prize acting on contested allegations about how a text was produced, not a case of a system failing in operation. The only technical claim in the record is a detector score, and the decision that followed was institutional rather than automated: the Académie Goncourt reviewed the allegations and removed the novel from its longlist. The publisher has halted promotion while stating it cannot confirm whether AI was used, which places the actual question, authorship, still unresolved.

The failure mode here, if one occurred, is authorship misattribution, a person presenting machine-generated text as their own. The facts do not show that. What they show is a detector output being treated as evidence, and a prize body choosing to act before the underlying question was settled. Catching this reliably would require provenance that does not depend on a classifier score, such as drafting records or process evidence, because a percentage from a detector is not a finding about who wrote a book.

It is not established that Orélien used AI, that the plagiarism examples are genuine, or that the detector's score is accurate. The allegations are allegations, and Orélien and his French publisher deny them.

reports.title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

summary:
The Prix Goncourt removed Canadian author Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était ça ou mourir from its longlist after reviewing allegations that he used AI to write it. The Académie Goncourt also cited examples of alleged plagiarism in his earlier work, first reported by Montreal newspaper La Presse. The novel, Orélien’s first, had sold to 23 countries and was set for English publication in 2028. His publisher, Les Editions du Boréal, has halted promotion but said it cannot confirm whether AI was used.

Orélien and his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, deny the allegations, which followed a post claiming the AI detector Pangram gave the novel a 100 per cent AI score. Orélien said he is angry and has always loved writing. The prize will be awarded in early November.
